candidates.headline: Pruning after profiling does not reduce profiling cost, which the neighborhood bound was introduced to limit
candidates.claim: Tbase pruning shrinks only the MILP, which already solves in seconds. It cannot reduce the profiling cost, which is set by candidate generation and by deduplication of repeated chunk specifications.
candidates.paper_fact: Pruning removes all candidate pairs whose post-overlap cost exceeds Tbase, reducing the effective problem size by roughly 3–5×.
candidates.premise: Discarding a pair because its profiled cost exceeds Tbase requires that cost to have been measured already. The decision therefore comes after the expensive step.
candidates.inference: Pruning acts only after profiling, so it removes MILP variables but not profiling work. Table 4 shows all MILP solves take 0.34-4.22 s, versus profiling that peaks near 3,050 s. The tractability benefit of pruning is therefore small compared with the cost it does not touch, and the profiling budget depends on K and on structural deduplication.
candidates.toy_example: Illustrative only, not a measurement: if 10,000 pairs are profiled and 7,000 are then pruned, profiling time is still that of 10,000 pairs. Only the solver sees 3,000 variables.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If vp or the number of distinct chunk types grows, pair count scales as K^2 per edge. The profiling budget could be exceeded even though pruning keeps the MILP small.
candidates.critical_link: Whether profiling cost, not MILP size, is the scaling bottleneck as K and vp grow.
necessary_conditions: Pairs are pruned only after their post-overlap cost has been profiled.
Profiling time dominates solve time in the target configuration.
defeaters: Deduplication keeps the distinct-pair count small, as reported for the tested models (237-637 pairs).
Profiling can be parallelized across reference device groups.
do_not_infer: That current profiling exceeds the one-hour budget; the paper reports about 3,050 s at most.
That pruning is useless; it still reduces the MILP size.
That the planner is slow at the tested scales.
candidates.lens: L1/L7: guarantee scope, and cost location at larger scale

candidates.headline: A backbone order fixed offline by the list scheduler conflicts with routing-varied task durations that runtime bubble filling cannot reorder
candidates.claim: The backbone-first alignment is computed from offline-profiled stable durations. At runtime, the Dynamic Bubble Optimizer moves only movable tasks and leaves the planned backbone order unchanged. Routing skew can therefore turn the statically chosen gap-fit alignment into a suboptimal one that nothing corrects.
candidates.paper_fact: a Dynamic Bubble Optimizer fills routing-induced idle slots with eligible movable tasks, without changing partition boundaries or the planned order of backbone tasks
candidates.premise: A gap-fit heuristic's choices depend on the durations of the tasks it aligns. If MoE kernel durations shift per iteration, the best backbone interleaving can shift too.
candidates.inference: Static planning uses durations from an offline profile, and §6.4 isolates static plans with a mock router that uniformly distributes tokens. §3.2 says routing changes task durations and shifts idle slots in ways no static plan can predict. Only movable tasks such as Wgrad are re-placed at runtime, so any mis-alignment among backbone tasks from the fixed list-scheduler order persists. The 'within ~1% of ILP' result is evaluated on profiled durations only, not on this runtime regime.
candidates.toy_example: Illustration only, not a measurement: the plan aligns a forward combine (A2A) with a backward attention task on the assumption of balanced routing. If routing makes the hot-expert MLP 30% longer, the planned pairing leaves the comm stream idle, and a different backbone order would have filled it. DBO can insert a Wgrad task into the gap but cannot reorder the backbone.
candidates.conditional_consequence: Where routing skew is large, e.g., with sparse top-10-of-512 routing, the static scheduler's quality advantage over simpler alignment may be partly lost. Recovery is limited to what movable tasks can fill.
candidates.critical_link: Whether the optimal backbone order changes materially under realistic per-iteration token-load variation.
necessary_conditions: Task durations used by the scheduler come from offline profiles under assumed routing
Backbone order is fixed after static planning
Runtime duration variation is large enough to change the best alignment
defeaters: The backbone order is robust to the observed duration variation
Pool of movable tasks is large enough to absorb most idle slots, as the paper says the pool is typically well-provisioned in production
Deferral and DBO gains in production (e.g., 3.4–5.4%) already capture most of the loss
do_not_infer: That DBO is ineffective, since the paper reports measured iteration-time gains
That the static plan is unusable in production
That runtime backbone reordering would be cheap or safe

candidates.headline: Avoiding kernel fragmentation does not imply a simpler planning problem; inter-microbatch overlap conflicts with independent partitioning
candidates.claim: Choosing inter-microbatch coupling moves the difficulty from kernels to the planner. Which chunks pair up depends on the partition, and the post-overlap cost of each pair can only be known by scheduling it and measuring it on hardware. This produces the partition-overlap cycle that the paper then has to resolve. Intra-microbatch fusion would not create this cycle.
candidates.paper_fact: avoids this fragmentation but shifts the hard problem
candidates.premise: When overlap partners come from different chunks, partition boundaries decide which pairs co-execute. The cost of a stage then depends on its partners and cannot be summed in isolation.
candidates.inference: The cyclic dependency and the profiling and MILP machinery follow from the inter-microbatch design choice. Tessera's planner contribution is partly a cost of that choice, not only a response to heterogeneity.
candidates.conditional_consequence: For homogeneous models the planner adds machinery with little gain beyond boundary chunks. The paper's own Qwen3 gains lean on overlap and DBO, with the partitioner contributing mainly through non-uniform boundary chunks.
candidates.critical_link: Inter-microbatch pairing makes the stage cost pair-dependent, which requires profile-then-partition planning.
necessary_conditions: Overlap partners are chosen across chunks by the pipeline schedule.
Overlap efficiency varies across pairs, as in heterogeneous layer mixes.
defeaters: Planning cost is reported as bounded: profiling takes under an hour and the MILP solves in seconds.
In heterogeneous models the paper shows large gains from overlap-aware partitioning, so the planner is needed there.
do_not_infer: Do not infer that planning cost is prohibitive.
Do not infer that intra-microbatch fusion would handle heterogeneity better.
Do not infer that the partitioner is useless on Qwen3.

quotes.text: avoids this fragmentation but shifts the hard problem
Choosing a good partition, however, requires accurately estimating each combination’s post-overlap cost

candidates.mechanism: When overlap partners come from different chunks, partition boundaries decide which pairs co-execute. The cost of a stage then depends on its partners and cannot be summed in isolation. The cyclic dependency and the profiling and MILP machinery follow from the inter-microbatch design choice. Tessera's planner contribution is partly a cost of that choice, not only a response to heterogeneity.

candidates.headline: The fixed template's benefit at current scale does not guarantee the co-optimization gains persist when microbatches per pipeline shrink
candidates.claim: Warmup/cooldown cost is structural to the template, and exposed EP communication in those phases is not recovered by steady-state overlap. If scaling reduces microbatches per pipeline, that fixed share grows. The paper reports no experiment that varies microbatches per pipeline rank at fixed model and template.
candidates.paper_fact: Even in the favorable regime (the top bar of Fig. 10), 27% of EP communication remains exposed (819 ms), over 40% of which originates from warmup and cooldown phases.
candidates.premise: In interleaved 1F1B the bubble fraction scales roughly as (p-1)/(v·m), where p is the number of pipeline ranks, v the virtual stages per rank, and m the microbatches per rank. Warmup/cooldown work has few concurrent pairs to overlap. The M-divisible-by-K constraint also ties m to global batch size.
candidates.inference: At larger scale with fewer microbatches per rank, the steady-state phase that Tessera optimizes best shrinks as a share of iteration time, and the template's structural cost grows. Gains from the partitioner and overlap scheduler may then saturate. This is not tested. The paper does not report microbatch counts for the Table 2 workloads, so the effect cannot be checked from the text.
candidates.toy_example: Not a measurement: if warmup plus cooldown costs a fixed 0.9 s and steady state costs 9 s at m=16, halving m to 8 gives steady state 4.5 s, so the fixed part rises from about 9% to 17% of iteration time.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If m per pipeline falls with cluster size, the relative speedup from steady-state overlap and partitioning would fall, even though Tessera's planning cost stays flat.
candidates.critical_link: Steady-state improvements act on a share of iteration time that depends on m. The paper's evidence does not vary m.
necessary_conditions: Microbatches per pipeline rank decrease as scale increases
Warmup/cooldown cost does not shrink in proportion
defeaters: Data-parallel scaling can keep m constant
Interleaving depth (vp) can be raised to cut the bubble
The padding mechanism may support large m through global batch size choices
Qwen3-Next-XL's largest gain at 12,288 GPUs argues against a simple saturation story, though the paper does not isolate the cause
do_not_infer: Do not infer that gains have already saturated
Do not infer that the 20-33% results are overstated
Do not infer that m is small in the paper's workloads

candidates.headline: An unchanged computation graph does not guarantee unchanged reduction order when Wgrad runs on a background thread at runtime-chosen times
candidates.claim: The 'by construction' bitwise-equivalence argument assumes that moving tasks on the timeline cannot change floating-point accumulation order. Deferred Wgrad tasks run on a separate thread and are placed at runtime. If they accumulate into shared gradient buffers, the accumulation order could depend on timing. The paper's evidence is one deterministic-mode run, not an argument that covers every case.
candidates.paper_fact: Tessera modifies only when and where tasks execute on the device timeline; the computation graph, operator semantics, and reduction order are unchanged.
candidates.premise: Floating-point addition is not associative. Accumulating partial gradients into a shared buffer in a different order can change the result bitwise. Deterministic mode typically fixes ordering in a given configuration, and what it fixes depends on the implementation.
candidates.inference: If a deferred Wgrad task and another contribution (for example, another microbatch's Wgrad or a gradient reduction) write to the same buffer, then the time at which each runs could affect the order of accumulation. The paper does not say whether Wgrad accumulation targets are ordered by explicit dependencies or by timing. It also does not say whether the dynamic optimizer's runtime choices were active in the verification run. Without that, 'by construction' is not established for the dynamic path.
candidates.toy_example: Illustration only, not a measurement: in fp32, (1e8 + 1) + (-1e8) = 0, but (1e8 + (-1e8)) + 1 = 1. Two gradient contributions applied to a shared buffer in swapped order can therefore differ bitwise.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If deferred Wgrad accumulates into a shared buffer without an order-fixing dependency, then runs with different dynamic placements could produce bit-different gradients. The bit-identical result would then hold only for the configuration that was verified.
candidates.critical_link: Whether deferred or concurrent Wgrad writes to shared accumulators have an enforced order that is independent of runtime timing.
necessary_conditions: Wgrad or gradient-reduction tasks from different microbatches write to the same buffer
The accumulation order is determined by execution timing rather than by an explicit dependency
Runtime placement of movable tasks varies between runs
defeaters: Per-task output buffers are reduced later in a fixed order
Stream or event dependencies serialize the accumulation in plan order
The verification run already exercised dynamic bubble filling and showed identical trajectories
do_not_infer: Do not infer that the reported bit-identical loss trajectories are wrong
Do not infer that Tessera changes model quality
Do not infer that numerical divergence has been observed

candidates.headline: Shadow actions that satisfy schedule structure do not guarantee that the profiled overlap plan and balanced partition still hold for padded microbatches
candidates.claim: Tessera's partition and overlap schedule are chosen from profiled post-overlap costs of pairs in which both chunks run real computation. A shadow action skips computation. When padding places a shadow action opposite a real chunk in an overlap pair, the pair no longer has the profiled compute-communication profile. The plan's steady-state balance and the dynamic bubble optimizer's assumptions may be affected in the padded portion of the iteration.
candidates.paper_fact: Under the fixed template, Tessera targets the steady-state overlap opportunities that recur across microbatches: a selected edge with high profiled post-overlap cost would repeatedly expose a straggler.
candidates.premise: Overlap hides communication behind computation from another in-flight microbatch. A null operation supplies no computation to hide behind and sends only pseudo-tensors. Per-pair cost therefore depends on both sides being real work.
candidates.inference: For padded slots, the overlap pairs formed with shadow actions were presumably not among those profiled (the paper profiles real chunk pairs), so the plan's cost model does not describe them. Whether this matters depends on where in the schedule the padding lands and on how many such slots exist. The paper does not discuss interaction between padding and overlap-aware planning or the dynamic bubble optimizer.
candidates.toy_example: Illustration only, not a measurement: if a backward chunk's All-to-All is meant to hide behind a forward chunk's compute, but the forward counterpart is a shadow action, then the All-to-All has nothing to overlap with and is exposed for that slot. The net effect could be small if few slots are padded.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If padded slots are concentrated in warmup or cooldown regions, or are few, the effect on the profile-based plan is negligible and consistent with the ~0.5% overhead. If padding is substantial, imbalance or exposed communication in those slots could erode the gains of the overlap-aware plan.
candidates.critical_link: The profiled post-overlap costs are assumed to describe all slots, but shadow actions create pair types that profiling did not measure.
necessary_conditions: Shadow actions are scheduled in positions where they form overlap pairs with real chunks
The execution plan's per-pair schedules were synthesized and profiled only for real chunk pairs
The number of padded slots is non-negligible
defeaters: Shadow actions are placed only where no overlap pair is formed, such as pipeline ends
The plan file for padded configurations is profiled with shadow actions included
The ~0.5% overhead already reflects any such loss
do_not_infer: Do not infer that padding degrades throughput by more than the reported 0.5%
Do not infer that the plan is invalid under padding
Do not infer where the paper places shadow actions in the schedule; this is not stated
candidates.lens: Interaction between a structural-padding mechanism and a planner whose cost model assumes real work on both sides of each overlap pair

candidates.headline: Profiling post-overlap cost on a 64-GPU reference group does not guarantee that the selected bottleneck edge is the real bottleneck at 8K-12K GPUs
candidates.claim: The partitioner picks the partition that minimizes the maximum profiled pair cost. The pair costs come from a small reference group, so the selection is only as valid as the profile is representative of production conditions.
candidates.paper_fact: Network congestion and switch contention cause stochastic variation in pipeline communication latency, both across iterations and across ranks.
candidates.premise: A MILP that minimizes a maximum over measured edge costs is sensitive to the relative ordering of those costs. Congestion, routing skew, or EP width that differ from the profiling environment can change this ordering. Even a few percent of error on one pair can change which edge is the maximum.
candidates.inference: A pair profiled as the cheapest or most balanced on the 64-GPU group could run slower under production jitter or skew. The chosen partition would then be balanced against a stale cost table.
candidates.toy_example: Illustrative only, not a measurement: edges X and Y are profiled at 100 ms and 98 ms. Production jitter adds 5% to the communication-heavy pair Y, so Y becomes 103 ms and is the true bottleneck, while the solver treated X as the bottleneck.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If production contention or skew differs from the reference-group profile, then the selected bottleneck edge and partition boundary may be suboptimal. The measured gains would then be a lower bound only if the profile happens to be representative.
candidates.critical_link: The profile taken on the 64-GPU group must preserve the ranking of the pairs that are near the maximum in production.
necessary_conditions: Production network noise or routing skew differs enough from the reference group to change pair costs by more than the gaps between near-maximum edges.
The perturbed pairs lie on or near the bottleneck of the MILP.
defeaters: Dynamic Bubble Optimizer absorbs part of the residual mismatch at runtime.
Cost gaps between the top candidate partitions are larger than the jitter-induced error.
Overlap efficiency is a stable property of a pair across scales.
do_not_infer: Do not infer that the reported 20%-33% gains are wrong.
Do not infer that the profiling approach performs worse than analytic estimation.
Do not infer that the paper measured the reference-to-production mismatch.

candidates.headline: Balancing the maximum steady-state post-overlap pair cost does not imply minimizing end-to-end iteration time
candidates.claim: The planner's objective covers only the steady-state overlap edges. Warmup and cooldown exposure is outside the optimized quantity, even though the paper shows it is a large part of the residual exposed communication.
candidates.paper_fact: Tessera therefore uses the maximum selected post-overlap edge cost as a surrogate objective for partition selection.
candidates.premise: Interleaved 1F1B has warmup and cooldown phases whose structure depends on the number of microbatches and the stage layout. A fixed per-pair maximum does not model these phases. As the number of microbatches shrinks, their share of the iteration grows.
candidates.inference: Two partitions with equal steady-state bottleneck cost can differ in warmup and cooldown cost, and the objective cannot tell them apart. With fewer microbatches per iteration, the surrogate will mis-rank partitions more often.
candidates.toy_example: Illustrative only, not a measurement: partitions P and Q both have a 100 ms maximum pair cost. P has 30 ms more warmup and cooldown exposure than Q. The MILP treats them as equal.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If warmup and cooldown share rises, for example with fewer microbatches at larger scale, then the partition chosen by the steady-state surrogate may sit further from the true optimum.
candidates.critical_link: The partition's effect on warmup and cooldown exposure must be uncorrelated with, or ignored by, its steady-state maximum pair cost.
necessary_conditions: Warmup and cooldown exposure differs among partitions that tie or nearly tie on the steady-state maximum.

defeaters: The partitions near the optimum have similar warmup and cooldown structure.
The microbatch count stays large, which keeps the steady-state share dominant.

candidates.headline: Minimizing the maximum post-overlap edge cost does not guarantee minimizing pipeline iteration time
candidates.claim: The MILP minimizes Tdom, the largest single overlap-edge cost. The authors state that iteration time depends on the full critical path. A partition with the lowest max edge can therefore still have a longer iteration than another feasible partition.
candidates.paper_fact: Pipeline iteration time depends on the full critical path through the fixed schedule.
candidates.premise: A min-max objective over individual edges does not account for how edge costs accumulate along the dependency chain. It also does not account for cross-rank waits, or for warmup and cooldown phases where few edges recur.
candidates.inference: Two partitions can have the same or a better Tdom and still differ in iteration time. This happens when the non-bottleneck edges, stage imbalance outside the pairs, or the warmup/cooldown path differ between them. The paper reports no check that Tdom ranks candidate partitions in the same order as measured iteration time.
candidates.toy_example: Illustration only, not a measurement: partitions P and Q both have a max edge of 10 ms. P's other edges are 2 ms each and Q's are 9 ms each. A critical path crossing many edges is longer under Q, but the objective ranks them equal.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If warmup/cooldown or cross-rank waits take a large share of iteration time, a Tdom-optimal plan may leave a large part of the available gain unrealized.
candidates.critical_link: Whether the single worst steady-state edge tracks the whole critical path across candidate partitions.
necessary_conditions: Candidate partitions differ in non-bottleneck edge costs or in stage-level imbalance.
Warmup, cooldown, or cross-rank waits are a non-trivial share of iteration time.
defeaters: The bottleneck edge dominates the critical path in the target regime, so ranking by Tdom matches ranking by iteration time.
The candidate neighborhood is so small that all candidates share nearly the same non-bottleneck structure.
do_not_infer: Do not infer that the surrogate performs poorly in practice. The paper reports end-to-end gains.
Do not infer that an alternative objective such as a sum or a critical-path model would do better.

candidates.headline: A max-edge-optimal partition does not carry over when the pipeline schedule template changes
candidates.claim: The overlap graph, the overlap edges, and the steady-state recurrence assumption are all derived from a fixed schedule template. The partition selected for one template is therefore optimal only for that template.
candidates.paper_fact: Tessera fixes the high-level pipeline schedule (e.g., interleaved 1F1B) and co-optimizes partitioning and overlap scheduling within it.
candidates.premise: In a graph-labeling formulation, the edge set E and the edge costs depend on which operations the schedule places concurrently on a rank. Changing the schedule, the number of virtual stages, or the microbatch regime changes the graph and the costs, so the old optimum is no longer an optimum of the new problem.
candidates.inference: Template parameters such as virtual stages per rank or the schedule type are outside the joint optimization. A partition tuned for one setting may be suboptimal after such a change. If the number of microbatches is too small for steady-state edges to recur, the surrogate's recurrence assumption also weakens.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If vp, the schedule, or the microbatch count changes after planning, the profile-then-partition pipeline must be re-run. The paper only describes the planner for a given template.

candidates.headline: Safety of Tbase pruning does not imply optimality of the returned partition
candidates.claim: Profile-guided pruning is safe only relative to Tbase and to the candidate neighborhood fixed beforehand. The returned partition is optimal only inside that neighborhood around the serial-balanced baseline, not over all contiguous partitions.
candidates.paper_fact: In practice, this significantly reduces the MILP size while preserving all solutions with Tdom ≤Tbase.
candidates.premise: A MILP only finds the optimum of the candidate set it is given. If candidates are generated by perturbing a baseline, any better partition outside the perturbation radius is never evaluated or profiled.
candidates.inference: Pruning removes only pairs worse than the baseline, and candidate generation removes everything outside the neighborhood. The reported gain is therefore a lower bound on what the overlap-aware objective could achieve. The paper does not say how close the neighborhood optimum is to the global one.
candidates.toy_example: Illustrative only, not a measurement: suppose the best partition shifts a stage boundary by 6 layers but candidates are limited to ±2. The solver returns the best ±2 plan, and the 6-shift plan is never profiled.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If the best overlap-aware partition lies outside the neighborhood, for example under extreme attention asymmetry, Tessera returns a baseline-adjacent plan and its reported gain understates the achievable one.
candidates.critical_link: Whether good overlap-aware partitions lie within the bounded neighborhood of the serial-balanced baseline.
necessary_conditions: The best post-overlap partition differs from the serial-balanced baseline by more than the candidate perturbation range.
No candidate inside the neighborhood has an equal or lower Tdom.
defeaters: The neighborhood is wide enough to contain the global optimum for the tested models.

candidates.headline: Matching GPU type and interconnect pattern does not guarantee that cached reference-group costs hold on congested production ranks

candidates.headline: An offline-profiled token-to-duration mapping does not guarantee accurate idle-window sizes under hardware interference
candidates.claim: Slot sizing combines observed token counts with an offline-profiled schedule. The paper itself reports that the idealized schedule deviates from silicon, so a sizing error can arise that is invisible to the count exchange and is not quantified for DBO.
candidates.paper_fact: Using the observed token distribution and the offline-profiled static schedule, Tessera estimates the fillable idle window bβ at each pre-annotated target slot β.
candidates.premise: A duration estimate derived from a profile is only as accurate as the profile's match to runtime conditions such as SM contention, kernel versions, and interference. Overestimating a window leads to injecting a task that does not fit, which extends the critical path.
candidates.inference: The paper reports an average ~5% theory-to-silicon deviation for overlap pairs, and primitive-level profiling reaches 15% in tail cases. candidates.toy_example: Not a measurement: if an estimated 1.0 ms window is really 0.85 ms and a 0.95 ms Wgrad task is injected, the pair's makespan grows by 0.1 ms.

candidates.headline: Per-slot greedy scoring does not imply a good global assignment of Wgrad tasks to slots
candidates.claim: DBO picks the highest-scored feasible task for each slot independently as slots arrive. It does not optimize the assignment of the whole movable pool to all slots in an iteration, and the paper does not compare DBO's greedy rule with a global solver.

candidates.premise: Online greedy packing of items into bins of differing sizes can be suboptimal. Taking an item now can remove the only item that would fit a later bin, and urgency terms in the score can override fit.
candidates.inference: Because the score mixes duration fit with deadline slack, an urgent small task can occupy a large slot that a large, less urgent task would have filled well. candidates.conditional_consequence: If slot sizes vary widely within an iteration and the pool holds tasks of heterogeneous durations, the filled fraction of idle time may fall below what a global assignment would reach.
candidates.critical_link: Greedy per-slot selection by a local score is not shown to approximate a global fill of the idle time; the ILP comparison applies to the static scheduler only.

candidates.headline: A per-GPU task-count cap on the movable-task pool does not guarantee a bound on deferred-activation memory
